newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe central banker criticises speculators.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe central banker criticises speculators.

text.p: Zimbabwe's central bank chief Leonard Tsumba has blamed local speculators for the recent volatile trade on the southern African country's foreign exchange market, a charge hotly denied by dealers.

"The simple act of trading on the back of rates quoted by other banks, without supporting or underlying transactions, should be avoided at all costs," Tsumba told the Foreign Currency Association (FCA) annual meeting in the eastern town of Nyanga.

"Quotations which bear no relation to real transactions and are simply designed to protect positions or to attract customers have the effect of distorting the resultant intervention action," he said in a speech made available on Wednesday.
The Zimbabwe dollar, pressured by what dealers said was import demand, fell 3.37 percent against the U.S. dollar between July and August, its sharpest decline since its January 1994 flotation.
It has since stabilised at around Z$10.20 to the U.S. dollar after central bank intervention.

Dealers blamed the steepness of the fall, and resultant wide spreads on quotations, on delayed Reserve Bank intervention, but Tsumba, citing market movements on September 2, said speculation was clearly evident.
He said on that day, the central bank bought some U.S.$2.5 million in "excess" foreign exchange after the Zimbabwe dollar had "appreciated" 0.8 percent against the U.S. unit.
Even after that intervention the market returned a surplus of U.S.$13.9 million. But the Zimbabwean dollar, instead of closing weaker, ended stronger.

"The message is clear and simple - rates quoted by the banks should always be relevant, meaningful and reflective of actual as well as expected flows, and positions of particular banks. Don't hide information from us as this hurts you and the system."
However, outgoing Foreign Currency Association chairman Andy Hodges denied the governor's allegations saying in a declining market banks had to protect their positions and their clients.

"I think there is a point of contention on his statement that banks or industries or whatever people are speculating in terms of the exchange rate movement over the last couple of weeks," Hodges told Zimbabwe state television on Tuesday night.

To guard against future wild movements in the exchange rate, Tsumba announced that all banks were now required to post with the central bank loan commitments in excess of U.S.$250,000 six months before they are due.
Analysts say the dollar, which declined 6.9 percent in the last quarter of 1995, is set to weaken further from October when tobacco sales, a source of steady foreign exchange inflows, close.
